title: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC
story:
A classifier makes two kinds of mistake. It flags something that was not there, and it misses something that was. These have different consequences in every real application — a false alarm on a fraud system costs a customer's afternoon, a miss costs the money — and a single proportion of correct answers adds them together and reports the sum, which is exactly the information you needed to keep separate.

Everything worth knowing here follows from four counts. Of the cases you flagged, how many were real and how many were not; of the cases you did not flag, how many were real and how many were not. Every measure in the title is a ratio of those four numbers, and the useful question about any of them is which denominator it uses.

Precision divides by what you flagged: of everything the model called positive, what fraction was. It answers the question a person acting on the output has — if I investigate this queue, how much of my time is wasted. Recall divides by what was actually there: of all the real cases, how many did we catch. It answers the question the person accountable for misses has. The two move against each other as you shift the threshold, because flagging more catches more and is wrong more often, and reporting one without the other is the most common way to describe a classifier misleadingly.

The single-number summaries exist because two numbers are awkward to compare. Their harmonic mean penalises imbalance between them, which is reasonable and still a choice — it weights the two errors equally, and you almost never care about them equally. The threshold-free summaries go further and integrate over every threshold, which is genuinely useful for comparing models and hides the thing you must eventually decide, since deployment requires one threshold and the summary averaged over all of them.

Davis and Goadrich established how the two curve spaces relate, in 2006: a curve dominates in one space if and only if it dominates in the other. That equivalence is exact and is narrower than it sounds, because they also showed that linear interpolation between points is incorrect in precision-recall space, and that algorithms optimising the area under one curve are not guaranteed to optimise the area under the other. Dominance transfers; area does not. Their summary of when to use which is the practical rule: when the class distribution is close to uniform the first kind has many desirable properties, but on a highly skewed dataset the second gives a more accurate picture — which is the subject of the next lesson.

problem.name: Classification metrics
problem.shape: A classifier's quality has to be reduced to a number, and it makes two kinds of mistake with different consequences.
tell: one number is being quoted for a classifier
precision is reported without recall or the reverse
a threshold-free summary is quoted and no threshold has been chosen
the two errors have obviously different costs and the metric treats them alike
problem.move: Start from the four counts rather than from a metric name, and pick the measure whose denominator matches the question being asked. Report precision and recall together, state the threshold, and choose that threshold from the relative cost of the two errors rather than from whichever value maximises a summary.
problem.invariant: Every one of these measures is a ratio of the same four counts, and they differ only in what they divide by. Which denominator is right is a question about who is acting on the output.
problem.breaks: Dominance in one curve space implies dominance in the other, but the areas are not interchangeable — linear interpolation is invalid in precision-recall space, and optimising the area under one curve does not guarantee optimising the area under the other. So the equivalence people rely on transfers less than it appears to.

cost.beats: a single proportion of correct answers, which sums two errors with different costs, and any single summary, which fixes a weighting between them that you did not choose deliberately

worked.reasoning:
The one whose denominator matches the decision being made — which means the question cannot be answered without knowing what happens to the output.

Every measure here is a ratio of the same four counts: flagged and real, flagged and not real, unflagged and real, unflagged and not real. They differ only in what they divide by, and that divisor encodes a question.

Precision divides by what you flagged. It answers the question of whoever acts on the output: of the cases arriving in this queue, how many are worth my time. If the cost of the work is per flagged item, this is the number that matters.

Recall divides by what was really there. It answers the question of whoever is accountable for misses: of everything that was actually happening, how much did we catch. If the cost is per missed case, this is the number that matters.

The two trade off directly against each other through the threshold, since flagging more catches more and is wrong more often. So reporting one alone is not a partial answer, it is a misleading one — any recall is achievable by flagging everything.

The harmonic mean of the two is the usual compromise, and I would be careful to present it as a choice rather than a neutral summary: it weights the two errors equally, and almost nobody cares about them equally. If the costs are known even roughly, a weighted version, or the expected cost itself, is more honest.

Threshold-free summaries answer a different question again — how good is the ranking, independent of where you cut. That is the right question when comparing models before a threshold exists, and the wrong one at deployment, where you must pick a single threshold and the summary averaged over all of them.

Two technical points I would raise because they are easy to get wrong. The two curve spaces are related by an exact result — a curve dominates in one if and only if it dominates in the other — but the areas are not interchangeable: linear interpolation between points is incorrect in precision-recall space, and an algorithm optimising one area is not guaranteed to optimise the other. And on skewed data the choice between them is not stylistic, because when the distribution is close to uniform the first has many desirable properties while on a highly skewed dataset the second gives a more accurate picture.

So my answer is: report the pair, state the threshold and the base rate, and quote a summary only alongside them.

problem.practice: Take a classifier and produce the four counts at three different thresholds. Compute precision and recall at each, and note how far apart they move. Then work out, for your actual application, roughly how many false alarms you would trade for one prevented miss — and check which threshold that implies.

beats.broke: A classifier makes two kinds of mistake, they have different consequences, and a single proportion of correct answers adds them together and reports the sum.
beats.fix: Count the four cells separately and build the measures that answer specific questions — how many flagged items were right, how many real cases were caught — then choose by which error is costly.
beats.cost: Each measure answers one question and ignores the others, threshold-free summaries hide the threshold you will actually have to pick, and improving the area under one curve does not guarantee improving the area under another.

interview.trap: Naming one. The question cannot be answered without knowing what happens to the output, since each measure differs only in its denominator and each denominator encodes a different person's question.

takeaway: Every one of these numbers is the same four counts over a different denominator, and the right denominator is decided by who acts on the output — so a single metric is not a summary of a classifier, it is a choice about whose error matters.
